data.title: Our church has a $1.5 million bequest earning 3.75% in a savings account. Are we throwing money away?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'Given the size and long-term nature of this gift, we want to make sure the funds are managed prudently'

"Our concern is that this rate of return may barely keep pace with inflation." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

A Catholic church in central Massachusetts recently received a $1.5 million bequest from a generous parishioner who has passed away. Under the current arrangement, the bank holding the funds will distribute 4% annually for 25 years.

We understand that the funds are currently invested in a savings account earning 3.75%. Our concern is that this may barely keep pace with inflation, and there may be better investment options available to the church.

We would greatly appreciate your thoughts and insights on several questions:

-- How should the church consider investing these assets to balance growth, preservation of principal and the need for annual distributions? Should the church require the bank to enter into a formal fiduciary agreement, and what protections would that provide?

-- Would it be preferable for the bank to distribute the funds quarterly, semiannually or annually? What are the potential risks and advantages of having the bank continue to manage the funds compared with engaging another financial institution or investment management company?

-- Should the church arrange for periodic independent financial audits of the fund? Would it be advisable for the church to retain a CPA, financial adviser, or investment professional to provide independent oversight?

Given the size and long-term nature of this gift, we want to make sure the funds are managed prudently and in the best interests of the parish and its future parishioners.

A Parishioner

Don't miss: 'My main goal is to help people': I'm single, 74, with $10 million burning a hole in my pocket. What should I do?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

No doubt this gift has raised a lot of questions, not least how to spend it.

Dear Parishoner,

Your church must have provided that parishioner with a great sense of community and spiritual healing to inspire such a generous gift.

No doubt it has raised a lot of questions, not least how to spend it. If that $1.5 million was put in a trust with instructions on how it should be distributed and invested over time, your church - as the beneficiary - may have less control over the interest rate. That would be up to the trustee. If, however, the money was given outright and the trustee are board members of your church, that's a different story. But you are correct: the consumer price index hit 3.7% in September.

A 3.75% interest rate is not a bad rate for a certificate of deposit (CD) or high-yield savings account, and slightly below what you might get for a 1-year Treasury bill. For a gift such as this, the church board or trustee is likely to prioritize safety over returns. Brian Katz, chief investment officer at Prosperity Wealth Management, agrees that 3.75% is a competitive rate. "The real question, which can only be answered by the church's decision makers, is how much risk they are willing to take," he told me.

"Given the long time horizon of 25 years and the relatively low disbursement rate of 4%, the portfolio has the leeway to take on more risk," he says. "One idea for a little higher yield without adding too much incremental risk would be an ultrashort bond fund. These can be found in both ETF and mutual fund structures. Currently, you can likely find something that yields 4.0% to 4.25%. As I said before, given the time horizon, building a diversified portfolio that includes equities, bonds, and cash may be considered, depending on the church's risk tolerance."

Don't miss: I'm a single 58-year-old veteran in California with $1.5 million and a VA pension. Can I retire?

Stock-market exposure

There's probably room for some stock-market exposure. "A conservative allocation of 20% equities and 80% bonds and cash wouldn't expose the portfolio to too much risk and should allow for a modestly higher return profile," Katz adds. "By focusing your equity investments on funds that favor high-quality or dividend-paying equities, the church could reduce the risk of the overall portfolio. The bond portfolio could include funds that purchase short-to-intermediate-term bonds, which would offset some of the duration risk."

The timing of distributions, if you have control over it, depends on how the church's finances are structured, but the longer you leave the money invested, the better the potential return. "The question on timing of the distributions should be made in consideration of the church's operating budget," Katz says. "From an investment standpoint, the longer the money remains invested, the more the investor benefits from compounding returns. Therefore, taking it out once at the end of the year can maximize the expected return of the portfolio."

You may also decide to use some of this money as an emergency fund, in case the church needs to replace the roof or - if you carry out broader renovations - is required to upgrade the entranceway or access to the restrooms to meet city standards. "The church should have an investment committee and a charter that defines the committee's roles and responsibilities," Katz adds. "Hiring an adviser is not a bad idea." In principle, a trust can be structured so that part of the investment income is distributed to a church while another part is reinvested.

It all depends on how the $1.5 million is held, who controls it, and what restrictions govern its use.

data.title: What gave this city its 'best place to retire' crown? You can actually afford to live there.
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

This Midwestern city came in first for the second year in a row

Someone turning 65 today can expect to live nearly two more decades, meaning Americans need to carefully select where to retire.

The cost of living is top of mind for Americans of all ages, cementing Midland, Mich., as the best place to retire for the second year in a row.

The Midwestern city of about 42,500 people held on to its top spot due to its low cost of living, high quality of life and favorable retiree taxes, according to the latest ranking by U.S. News & World Report.

"The whole country is feeling the pinch right now, so it's not a surprise that affordability is a top priority," Megan Wood, managing editor of home services and real estate at U.S. News, told MarketWatch.

Midland's affordability metrics looked at items such as the cost of shelter, including rents and mortgages, as well as utilities, transportation and fuel and consumer goods and services. The city does not impose a local sales or income tax, and Michigan does not tax Social Security income.

Last year, Midland nabbed the top spot due to quality of life, as well as affordability. Its top ranking this year was driven by affordability. Midland's community is active, with abundant senior programming for social and cultural events, as well as many options for senior housing, Wood said. About 23% of its residents are over the age of 45 and 20% are over age 65.

The city, which is about two hours from Detroit and near Lake Huron's Saginaw Bay, is the headquarters of chemical company Dow (DOW). In addition to its thriving arts and cultural scene, Midland is known for an abundance of midcentury modern architecture. It's also home to the minor league baseball team the Great Lakes Loons.

"Retirees are seeking a place that gives them a sense of security and comfort as they live out their golden years," Wood said. "Whether that comfort prioritizes scenic nature spots, access to multicultural experiences, or everyday affordability, places like Midland, Michigan, offer financial safety while still providing a good quality of life."

U.S. News adjusted its scoring weights for the new rankings to mirror growing concerns over affordability in the United States. This resulted in multiple double-digit jumps among the top 25, including No. 8 Paducah, Ky., landing in the top 10 for the first time.

The report comes as roughly 18% of the U.S. population is now 65 or older. An adult turning 65 today can expect to live nearly two more decades, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That puts increased importance on the decision about where to retire, since retirement itself could last decades.

More than one in three retirees have moved during retirement, according to 2025 research by the nonprofit Transamerica Institute and the Transamerica Center for Retirement Studies. Among those who moved, the top reasons included being closer to family and friends, downsizing into a smaller home, starting a new chapter in life, reducing expenses, moving to a place with a better climate and no longer needing to live near work, Transamerica found.

Midland is followed on the list by Homosassa Springs, Fla., which is bolstered by its strong affordability scores, growth of its older population and low retiree taxes. Weirton, W. Va., came in at No. 3 with high marks for quality of life, low retiree taxes, affordability and quality of life.

Traditional retiree hotspots such as Florida and Texas each appeared twice in the top 10 and multiple times throughout the listing of the top 250 locales, while states such as California and New Jersey fell toward the bottom of the list due to their high cost of living, Wood said.

U.S. News evaluated more than 850 U.S. cities based on how well they meet American retirees' expectations against measures including quality of life, affordability, healthcare, retiree taxes, job market, and population and migration for retirees ages 55 and older.

"This ranking is meant to be used as a starting point for retirees to do more research and find the best place that suits them," Wood said.

Other rankings of the best places to retire earlier this year highlighted Florida, with Orlando taking the top spot in WalletHub's recent study due to favorable taxes and access to quality healthcare. Meanwhile, Wyoming topped a report by CareScout, a company that helps families find eldercare, due to the state's lack of personal income tax and its having lowest rate in the nation of multiple chronic conditions among Medicare beneficiaries.

-Jessica Hall

RADNOR, Pa., Oct. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP (www.ktmc.com), a nationally recognized securities litigation law firm, informs investors that a securities fraud class action lawsuit has been filed against Fluence Energy, Inc. (Fluence Energy) (NASDAQ: FLNC) on behalf of those who purchased or acquired Fluence Energy securities between November 24, 2025 and September 16, 2026, inclusive. The lawsuit is filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and is captioned Hatweek v. Fluence Energy, Inc., No. 1:26-cv-08475 (S.D.N.Y.).  Investors have until November 27, 2026, to file for lead plaintiff status. 

CONTACT KTMC TO DISCUSS YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS:    
If you purchased or acquired Fluence Energy securities and have lost money on your investment, please provide your information here: https://www.ktmc.com/flnc-fluence-energy-inc-class-action-lawsuit?utm_source=PR_Newswire&utm_medium=pressrelease&utm_campaign=flnc&mktm=PR 

You can also contact attorney Jonathan Naji, Esq. by calling (484) 270-1453 or by email at info@ktmc.com.  There is no cost or obligation to speak with an attorney.

To view the Fluence Energy video on YouTube, click here: https://youtu.be/Hmn8AUJTqQQ 

FLUENCE ENERGY, INC. CLASS ACTION LAWSUIT - COMPLAINT ALLEGATION SUMMARY:
The complaint alleges that, throughout the Class Period, Defendants made materially false and/or misleading statements, as well as failed to disclose material facts about the company's business, operations, and prospects. Specifically, Defendants misrepresented and/or failed to disclose that: (1) Fluence Energy's ability to deliver its backlog and recognize the revenue underlying its fiscal 2026 guidance depended on new contract manufacturing facilities, including facilities that were not completed, not operational, and/or not capable of producing at the volumes the company's guidance assumed; (2) the corrective measures Fluence Energy had implemented to address production problems at its contract manufacturers were not resolving those problems, which continued and extended to the company's new facilities; and (3) as a result of the foregoing, Defendants' statements about the company's business, operations, and prospects were materially false and misleading and/or lacked a reasonable basis at all relevant times.

Why did Fluence Energy's Stock Drop?
On February 4, 2026 and August 5, 2026, Fluence Energy reported disappointing quarterly financial results, including GAAP gross profit margin declines, an increase in net losses, and weaker than expected revenue.  As a result, Fluence Energy's stock price fell significantly and the company slashed its fiscal year 2026 revenue guidance and its adjusted EBITDA guidance.

Then, on September 16, 2026, Fluence Energy announced through a mid-quarter guidance update that the company was cutting its full year revenue guidance by approximately $600 million to $2.4 billion. Additionally, Fluence Energy further cut its full year adjusted EBITDA guidance from negative $10 million to negative $200 million, attributed to "delays in the ramp-up of our contract manufacturing facility."  On this news, Fluence Energy's stock price fell $1.39 per share, or 15.36%, to close at $7.66 per share on September 17, 2026.

WHAT FLUENCE ENERGY, INC. INVESTORS CAN DO NOW:

  1. File to be lead plaintiff by November 27, 2026.
  2. Contact KTMC for a free case evaluation. All representation is on a contingency fee basis, there is no cost to you.
  3. Retain counsel of choice or take no action.

THE LEAD PLAINTIFF PROCESS FOR FLUENCE ENERGY, INC. INVESTORS:
Fluence Energy investors may, no later than November 27, 2026, seek to be appointed as a lead plaintiff representative of the class through Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP or other counsel, or may choose to do nothing and remain an absent class member. A lead plaintiff is a representative party who acts on behalf of all class members in directing the litigation.  The lead plaintiff is usually the investor or small group of investors who have the largest financial interest and who are also adequate and typical of the proposed class of investors. The lead plaintiff selects counsel to represent the lead plaintiff and the class and these attorneys, if approved by the court, are lead or class counsel. Your ability to share in any recovery is not affected by the decision of whether or not to serve as a lead plaintiff.

Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP encourages Fluence Energy investors to contact the firm for more information.

Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP (KTMC) is a leading U.S. plaintiff-side law firm focused on securities-fraud class actions and global investor protection. The firm represents individual investors as well as institutions, such as major pension funds, asset managers, and international investors. data.title: The S&P 500 isn't the big winner you may think it is
data.description:
By Brett Arends

The index's weakness may surprise a generation of investors raised on the cult of 'stocks always go up'

Are you feeling lucky?

Wall Street tries not to mention this too often, but there is about a 25% chance that your U.S. stock-market index fund, including an S&P 500 SPX large-cap fund, will prove to be a poor investment or worse over the next 10 years.

And there is even about a 1 in 7 chance, or 14%, that it will prove to be a poor investment over the next 20 years.

Which is remarkable, especially for a generation of investors who have been raised on the cult of "stocks for the long run," "don't time the market" and "stocks always go up."

Being a "permabear" and sitting in cash while predicting disaster is a foolish strategy over the long term. Being a "permabull" and always betting on stocks is slightly better, because stocks go up more than they go down - but it still leaves a lot to be desired.

The biggest myth is that somehow it doesn't really matter when you buy stocks, because over time they will always produce spectacular returns.

To see the actual numbers, I used the long-term stock-market data compiled by Yale finance professor Robert Shiller, whose work on markets and valuations earned him the Nobel Prize in economics. I used monthly data going back 100 years, to 1926. Technically, Shiller has data on stock-market returns and inflation going back to the 1870s, but there are reasons to be skeptical about the value - or even the reliability - of such ancient financial history. One-hundred years of monthly returns, adjusted for inflation, seems a pretty good sample, especially in an era when venture capitalists and Wall Street frequently refer to 10 or 20 years as "long term."

To cut to the chase: All this permabull mantra about stocks for the long term, and "average" stock-market returns of 6% or 7% a year plus inflation, need enormous caveats.

Averages can hide a lot of detail - like when Bill Gates walks into a bar and the "average" net worth of the occupants suddenly jumps into the billions of dollars.

On a 10-year view, the difference between buying into the S&P 500 at the best time and buying into it at the worst time was worth an astonishing 25% per year. Someone who invested in the summer of 1949 and held on for 10 years earned a spectacular compound return of 18.8% a year plus inflation - the equivalent of turning $10,000 into $56,000 in constant, inflation-adjusted dollars.

But someone who invested in the S&P 500 in the early spring of 1999 and held on for 10 years ended up losing on average 6% per year in constant, inflation-adjusted dollars - the equivalent of turning $10,000 into around $5,500 in real terms. In other words, they lost nearly half their entire investment in real, purchasing-power terms, plus a decade of compound positive returns on which they had been relying.

By coincidence, the terminal value after 10 years for someone picking the absolute worst moment to invest was almost exactly one-tenth the terminal value for the person who picked the best moment.

The variations over 20 years were smaller, but still huge. Someone who invested in the index in the spring of 1980 and held on for 20 years would have turned $10,000 into $128,000 - again, measured in constant, inflation-adjusted dollars. That's an annualized return of inflation plus 13% or more per year. But someone who made the same investment in the spring of 1962 - or September 1929, for that matter - and waited 20 years effectively earned nothing at all; the average annual return was about 0.3% a year.

The past is no guarantee of the future, and maybe these past patterns won't repeat themselves. But Wall Street seems very keen to cite historical data to suit its own purpose.

None of this is supposed to be an argument in favor of being a permabear and sitting on the sidelines in cash. Being a permabear is even more foolish than being a permabull, because the stock market has gone up far more often than it has gone down, especially over time. But it does mean that the permabulls, too, are viewing the world through a distorted lens.

When I ranked S&P 500 10-year returns by decile, I came up with the following:

In other words, 10% of the time over the past 100 years, investors in the S&P 500 lost an average of 2.6% a year, adjusted for inflation, over a 10-year period. That's the equivalent of losing 23% of your purchasing power over the full decade. Another 10% of the time, they earned an average total return of 0.4% a year - before taxes and fees, incidentally.

When I ranked the 20-year returns by decile, I got this:

The worst-case scenario isn't as bad, but it's still pretty lousy: 1.6% a year, or less than 40% total over 20 years. And that's before taxes and fees, of course.

Right now, you can earn an all-but-guaranteed 3.1% a year plus inflation for up to 30 years through inflation-protected Treasury bonds, or TIPS. In the past 100 years, investors in the S&P 500 did worse during 24% of all 10-year periods, and 14% of all 20-year periods.

That doesn't mean TIPS are the answer - but it does mean U.S. stocks don't deliver as often as the permabulls like to pretend.

-Brett Arends

data.title: Social Security's fate - and your benefits - are in the hands of the candidates elected this year
data.description:
By Alessandra Malito

The program is expected to run out of money in the next six years, which is the same amount of time as a senator's term

This election will be an important one for Social Security's future.

The dire warnings that Social Security is running out of money have been blaring for so long that they have started to sound like white noise. But the program's day of reckoning is approaching quickly, just as a new Congress is set to be elected.

The candidates elected to the Senate on Nov. 3 - one third of the chamber - will serve a six-year term beginning in January. Social Security's trust funds are expected to run out of money in six years.

With those timelines merging, and the Social Security Administration in dire need of reform, this year's elections are pivotal for the future of the program. The politicians voted in next week, including senators and representatives, may be those deciding the fate of American retirees' finances.

"This election comes at a critical moment for Social Security," said Rebecca Vallas, chief executive officer of the National Academy of Social Insurance, a nonpartisan nonprofit focused on social insurance programs. "The senators elected this November - and likely the president elected in 2028 - will be the leaders who determine what to do about Social Security's financing gap."

Social Security is on the path to insolvency. The program's trust funds are expected to be exhausted by 2032, at which point beneficiaries may see cuts of about 26% to their payments. Congress has never let Social Security falter or skip a benefit, but the federal government hasn't voted on any legislation that would resolve the program's financing issues.

Nearly 69 million people received Social Security benefits in September, according to the Social Security Administration. More than 57 million of them were 65 and older.

Some candidates are talking about Social Security. John Deaton, a Republican candidate for a Senate seat representing Massachusetts, said the program's problems highlight what's wrong with our current political system.

"Social Security is one of the examples of why we have a broken Congress. Everyone knows that in 2032 Social Security will not be able to make the current payments that it is making. They talk about it being bankrupt," Deaton said in an interview. "Whoever gets elected this cycle will have to deal with Social Security."

This isn't the first time Social Security has come dangerously close to insolvency. Legislators waited until the last minute to pass the Social Security Amendments of 1983, a package of provisions to stop the program from running out of money, including increasing its prescribed full retirement age from 65 to 67 through a long and phased process, implementing a tax on up to 50% of Social Security benefits, and delaying the cost-of-living adjustment by six months.

Legislators at the time expected those provisions to keep the program solvent until 2040, former Social Security Administration Commissioner John Svahn told MarketWatch last year. Svahn served as commissioner in the early 1980s, during its financing crisis. "It was recognized at the time that Congress would have to do something in between," he said. "Well, they haven't done it yet."

What's at stake

The Congressional Budget Office, a nonpartisan independent federal agency, released its latest projections in September, saying Social Security could become insolvent by 2032. At that point, Social Security recipients would see a 26% benefit cut. By the end of the century, if lawmakers do nothing to fix the problem, beneficiaries would see a 40% benefit cut.

For the average Social Security recipient, these cuts could represent hundreds of lost dollars. The average monthly benefit for a retired worker in September 2026 was $2,089 a month, meaning a 26% cut would reduce the monthly check by $543, without adjusting for inflation.

These estimates are even more severe than what the Social Security trustees suggested in June. The trustees also expect the money to run out in 2032 but estimated a 22% benefit cut. These cuts would be automatic, and they would hurt many current and future retirees.

At least 13.7% of older Americans rely on Social Security payments for 90% or more of their family income, according to a 2024 Census Bureau's Center for Economic Studies report.

Decades ago, retirement planning was likened to a "three-legged stool": one leg represented a pension, another leg represented Social Security and the last stood for the individual's own personal savings and investments.

Today, that stool is pretty wobbly. Pensions in the private sector have become almost obsolete, and Americans are struggling to cover everyday expenses, let alone save enough money for their old age. Almost half of Americans said they are "deprioritizing" or unable to save for retirement because of current expenses, according to a survey of 1,000 working adults 18 and older by NFP, a company focused on workforce operations. More than four in 10 employees 55 and older said they expect Social Security to be their primary source of income in retirement.

Social Security reform ideas have floated around Congress for decades. Legislators have introduced proposals through the years, and policy-advocacy groups and experts have written blueprints to reverse insolvency.

Common suggestions include eliminating the income-tax cap, raising the full retirement age, implementing new taxation avenues or altering the cost-of-living adjustment in an effort to boost revenue for the program. None of these options on their own would fully fund Social Security's shortfall, but a package of provisions might.

Eliminating the income-tax cap

Workers contribute 6.2% of their earnings to Social Security, and their employers contribute another 6.2% (self-employed individuals contribute the full 12.4%). Workers only pay Social Security taxes on income up to $184,500 this year. Any income that exceeds that cap is not subject to the tax.

One bipartisan proposal would eliminate that cap, so that all earners' income would be taxed for Social Security. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, and Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio, were the latest to suggest this option to help Social Security's finances, coming together earlier this year to tell Congress to lift the cap.

This proposal would hit higher earners, since nothing would change for those with earnings below the cap. Experts have suggested two ways to treat benefits if lawmakers eliminated the cap: one in which higher earners could later get benefits calculated using what they've contributed through the years and another in which Congress could cap their benefits regardless of how much they pay in tax.

Massachusetts candidate Deaton agreed that increasing the cap is one way to help the program. "It is not the only fix we need, but it is the most commonsense fix," he said.

Raise the retirement age

Another possibility would be to raise Social Security's full retirement age, which is currently 67 for anyone born in or after 1960. The full retirement age, or FRA, is the age at which beneficiaries receive 100% of what they're owed. Some retirees claim retirement benefits sooner - as early as age 62 - but doing so results in a permanent reduction to their monthly payments. Others might delay their benefits, which gives them an additional 8% in payments for every year they delay their FRA between 67 and 70.

Some candidates who ran in the 2024 presidential election floated raising the full retirement age as an option to shore up Social Security's finances, though with the expectation that the FRA would only rise for younger workers who have decades to go until retirement.

Increasing the FRA from 67 to 68 immediately would close the shortfall by 12%, and raising it to 69 would reduce it by 17%. Doing that, however, could derail the retirement planning of millions of Americans, as it could affect those in or near their Social Security-claiming years.

Other possible measures

Experts have also suggested new income streams through taxation, including directing some estate-tax revenue to Social Security, expanding on net investment income taxes and reaching beyond payroll taxes in the workplace.

Most of Social Security's revenue comes from payroll taxes, but the pay-as-you-go system is overworked. The worker-to-beneficiary ratio was 2.7 to 1 in 2023, according to Pew Research Center, far narrower than in 1965, when there were four times as many workers as there were beneficiaries. That ratio is forecast to drop to 2.1 by the end of the century. Wealth inequality has also widened the gap between low and high earners, affecting how many people are taxed on their entire earnings versus those who exceed the income-tax cap. Only about 83% of earnings are covered by the program, compared with 90% in 1983.

Salaries are just one portion of a worker's pay, however. The contributions employers make to their workers' retirement plans and workplace health insurance aren't subject to Social Security taxes, though experts have considered what implementing Social Security taxation on such benefits would do for the program. Applying the payroll tax to employer-sponsored health insurance, for instance, could generate $2.4 trillion over 10 years, according to the Tax Foundation.

Legislators have also considered the impact that taxing net investment income could have on the program. Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent, joined Democrat Warren in proposing a bill that included steeper taxes on higher earners' net investment income, which would include dividends, capital gains, rental income and interest. A combination of eliminating the income-tax cap, a new 12.4% tax on net investment income and a new net-investment-income tax on certain businesses could bring the program an additional $33.8 trillion, according to a letter written by Stephen Goss, former chief actuary of Social Security.

data.title: Social Security's fate - and your benefits - -2-
data.description:
One tax wouldn't affect beneficiaries or workers, at least not while they were alive. The current estate-tax exemption - $15 million for individuals, $30 million for married couples and an unlimited amount between spouses when one predeceases the other - is extremely high for the average person. Experts argue income from the federal estate tax, which is applied to estates with values above the exempted level, should go toward Social Security.

Robert M. Ball, who served as Social Security commissioner from 1962 to 1973, proposed an estate-tax exemption of $3.5 million and a 45% tax rate, with all revenue generated earmarked for the program.

The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is one of the biggest perks of Social Security, because it provides inflation protection so that retirees' purchasing power isn't diminished over their retirements. The COLA is calculated using a subset of the consumer-price index, currently the CPI-W, which tracks the costs of goods and services used by urban workers.

Proposals include switching to a chained COLA, which accounts for buyers' spending habits, such as switching from one protein to another when the first becomes more expensive. Former President Barack Obama included a plan to switch to chained COLA in his 2014 budget proposal but dropped it after pushback. Another idea is a straightforward reduction, by perhaps 0.5% or 1%.

What the candidates are saying

Social Security is a perennially contentious topic, unsurprisingly with so many people relying on it for so much of their retirement income. Politicians won't talk about the program or its insolvency often. That's why it is considered the "third rail" of politics.

Many candidates have said they want to "protect" and "strengthen" Social Security, or that Congress needs to take the problem seriously, but these sound bites usually don't include specifics or mentions of possible resolutions.

Others, however, have commented on proposals, such as eliminating the income-tax cap. One senatorial candidate opposed the increase, but 20 supported the increase and two were leaning toward it, according to an analysis from Jonathan Schwabish, a senior fellow focusing on taxation at the Urban Institute, an economic- and social-policy think tank, and analyst Zane Snyder Cox. Another 18 candidates had no statement.

Warren and Moreno's bipartisan effort dealing with the income-tax cap likely opened the door for discussion around Social Security during this election season, Schwabish said.

Still, there's much more about Social Security reform to discuss, and more conversations to be had in Congress to find a fix for the program's financial woes. "It hasn't spread to a wider conversation or more specific legislative language," Schwabish said. "We need to wait and see what will happen."

-Alessandra Malito

data.title: 'He was heartbroken': My husband's kids abandoned him when he was dying. Was he right to leave everything to me?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'In the end, he left them a few sentimental mementos, some collectibles and old photographs'

"I'm still angry with them for the way they treated their father, especially when he was dying and needed them most." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

My situation was the opposite of the one in this letter (My partner of 17 years left me his $1 million home. His children are livid. Am I obliged to split it with them?). When I met my husband, he had essentially been on his own for nearly 20 years. He was a wonderful father who helped his children in every way he could, and he was just as devoted to my kids - a true go-to guy. He was truly the love of my life.

For the last six years of his life, he was terminally ill, and I was his full-time caregiver, around the clock. My kids, who had homes and children of their own, would drop everything to help us whenever they could. His kids, on the other hand, were both single, childless adults in their 50s, yet they never lifted a finger. No matter how much he begged them to help us, they rarely called and didn't even visit him during the last three years of his life.

He was heartbroken by their careless indifference. In the end, he left them a few mementos, some collectibles and old photographs. I inherited everything else. I still gave both of his children some money, and I've set aside a portion of my portfolio for them as well, should it outlive me, because that's simply who I am. But I'm still angry with them for the way they treated their father, especially when he was dying and needed them most.

No father deserves that kind of indifference from his own children.

Wife, Mother and Now Widow

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My abusive ex-husband promised $20,000 for our kids' education. Now he refuses to pay. Is he legally obligated?

We should, for better or for worse, be wary of making judgments about how much someone's children did or did not care.

Dear Wife,

Sometimes the hardest thing to do in life is to accept people for who they are. And when it comes to inheritance, there's often no right or wrong answer.

The tension many people experience in relationships is the expectation that they will be somebody they're not or do something they will never do. This can last for years, even decades, and despite hopeful moments of decency and respite from perceived indifference, unreliable people will show you who they are time and again, if you let them. That is a tragedy when it comes to parents and children who will never meet each other's needs. It can also bring a measure of clarity.

Your late husband seems to have reached that painful realization during his chronic illness. He saw who showed up for him, and he could see with clear-eyed perspective, perhaps for the first time, who did not support him through that difficult time. For you, it must have been painful to witness, especially because you knew just how much your husband needed and wanted their love and support. An absence of kindness at such a vulnerable time is heartbreaking.

But that clarity can also be freeing. He could finally see, perhaps, the faithful people in his life, the people who showed up and, importantly, showed that they cared. It's possible to show up and tick a box but not actually do any emotional heavy lifting, like spending time with an ailing friend or relative one-on-one or even picking up the phone to say, "I was thinking about you. I'm just checking in." That can mean as much as offering a lift to the doctor's office or the salon.

Life after a chronic illness

We should, for better or for worse, also be wary about making judgments about how much his children did or did not care. Your husband acknowledged that relationship by leaving his children items with important sentimental value. Estrangement, fear of illness, an unresolved family saga, emotional anxiety and, yes, blunt avoidance can lead to hurtful behavior. Understanding why someone acted as they did can help foster compassion for others and, importantly, for oneself.

Oasis Hospice Care, which has facilities in Houston and Austin, explores the question: Why do some friends and loved ones disappear after a chronic illness diagnosis? "Many people genuinely care but feel uncomfortable discussing illness. They may worry about saying the wrong thing, making the situation worse, or triggering difficult emotions. Instead of reaching out imperfectly, some choose silence," the organization wrote. "Unfortunately, that silence can feel like abandonment."

Leaving his children items with important sentimental value honored their relationship and their history.

"For some friends, seeing someone they care about struggle can trigger fears about aging, disability, vulnerability, or mortality," it adds. "Rather than processing those emotions, they may unconsciously withdraw. Friendships often develop around shared experiences: traveling, dining out, sports, community events, active hobbies. When chronic illness limits participation in those activities, friendships sometimes struggle to adapt."

Friends and some family members who aren't willing to adjust to the new normal may slowly fade away, the organization says. "Many people report feeling shocked by who stays and who leaves. Sometimes casual acquaintances become incredible sources of support, while long-term friends disappear. It's important to remember that another person's inability to handle illness often reflects their limitations - not your worth."

Staying true to your convictions

Your own children showed up for your husband, and that must have meant everything. Anyone who experiences chronic illness and re-evaluates the relationships in their life will tell you that there are many gifts and revelations during that time; they may be surprising or disappointing at the time, but ultimately allow you to focus on the people who care about you. Your husband had many people who were there for him, and he adjusted his estate plan accordingly.

He stayed true to his convictions and did not bow to social pressure or pressure from family members to leave his children a substantial amount in his will. That was his decision to make, and he was entitled to distribute his estate as he saw fit. He had you, of course, but leaving his children items with important sentimental value honored their relationship and their history, without giving away a large chunk of his estate to people who did not show up during his time of need.

Your late husband had you, your own children, and other friends who chose to show up for him. As much as the absence of his own children hurt, you were all there for him, and he remembered that in his will. Your husband sounds like a stand-up guy and, honestly, plenty of people in your position would move on and leave their stepchildren nothing in their will. You are making sure you dignify those relationships, in your own way.

Perhaps it's a posthumous show of respect to the man you loved, and also a refusal to allow his children's behavior to turn you into someone you don't want to be.
